overview: This section covers how objects move between Amazon S3 storage classes and how Lifecycle Rules automate transitions, expiration, version cleanup and multipart-upload cleanup, filtered by prefix or tag. It also covers S3 Storage Class Analysis, the reporting tool that recommends when to move data to Standard IA. For SAA-C03 this is core Cost-Optimized storage design (managing S3 object lifecycles, storage tiering, selecting the data lifecycle), so expect scenario questions that give retention windows and retrieval-time requirements and ask you to pick storage classes plus a lifecycle design.

coreConcepts.definition: Moving an object from one S3 storage class to another (for example Standard to Standard IA to Glacier) without changing its key; can be automated with Lifecycle Rules.
The target class for infrequently accessed objects that must still be retrieved quickly; the storage class S3 Analytics makes recommendations about (together with Standard).
Archive classes for objects you do not need fast access to; Deep Archive is the deeper, cheaper archive tier used after a shorter-term archive step in the section's scenarios.
A rule action that moves objects to another storage class after a condition such as days since creation (e.g. move to Standard IA at 60 days, to Glacier after 6 months).
A rule action that deletes (expires) objects after some time, e.g. deleting access log files after 365 days.
An expiration action that deletes old versions of an object when versioning is enabled.
An expiration action that deletes incomplete Multi-Part uploads, avoiding storage charges for unfinished uploads.
A lifecycle rule scoped to a key prefix, e.g. s3://mybucket/mp3/* so only that folder of objects is affected.
A lifecycle rule scoped to object tags, e.g. Department: Finance, so rules follow business meaning rather than key path.
An S3 Analytics feature that monitors access patterns and produces a daily .csv report (storage class by object age) to help decide when to transition objects.

mustRemember: Transitions are between storage classes; Lifecycle Rules automate them.
Infrequently accessed objects: move to Standard IA. Archive objects without fast-access needs: Glacier or Glacier Deep Archive.
Transition actions and expiration actions are separate rule actions; a rule may have both.
Expiration actions can delete: current objects after N days, noncurrent (old) versions when versioning is enabled, and incomplete Multi-Part uploads.
Rules can filter by prefix (e.g. s3://mybucket/mp3/*) or by object tag (e.g. Department: Finance).
S3 Storage Class Analysis gives recommendations only for Standard and Standard IA.
S3 Analytics does NOT work for One-Zone IA or Glacier.
S3 Analytics report is updated daily; it takes 24 to 48 hours to start seeing data analysis.
S3 Analytics is a good first step to build or improve Lifecycle Rules — it is not an automation of transitions itself.

keyComparisons.difference: Both are for infrequently accessed data, but the section's thumbnail scenario uses One-Zone IA for easily recreated objects, so pick it when the data can be regenerated and Standard IA otherwise.
Deep Archive is the deeper archive step used after an earlier Glacier-class or Standard IA stage when the retrieval requirement is looser (hours rather than immediate).
Transition changes the storage class of an object that stays alive; expiration deletes the object (or old versions / incomplete uploads).
Prefix scopes by key path (s3://mybucket/mp3/*); tag scopes by object metadata (Department: Finance), which is better when the rule must follow objects regardless of key layout.

keyComparisons.items: S3 Storage Class Analysis vs Lifecycle Rules
keyComparisons.difference: Analysis only observes and reports on access patterns (recommendations for Standard and Standard IA only); Lifecycle Rules are what actually perform transitions and expirations.
With versioning enabled a delete is hidden by a delete marker, so old data is removed by expiring noncurrent versions, not by ordinary object expiration.

commonMisunderstandings: S3 Storage Class Analysis performs transitions for you — it does not; it produces recommendations that you then implement as Lifecycle Rules.
S3 Analytics can recommend Glacier transitions — it only covers Standard and Standard IA and does not work for One-Zone IA or Glacier.
Turning on versioning is enough to clean up old data — you must also expire noncurrent versions, or they keep accruing cost.
Deleting an object in a versioned bucket removes the data — it adds a delete marker; the object versions persist until noncurrent-version expiration.
Lifecycle rules can only target a whole bucket — they can be scoped by prefix or by object tag.
S3 Analytics gives instant results — allow 24 to 48 hours before analysis appears, and the report is updated daily.
mentalModels: Think of Lifecycle Rules as a conveyor belt: whenever an age/condition is met, an object moves to the next class or falls off (expire).
Think of S3 Storage Class Analysis as an X-ray of the bucket that tells you where to place the belt; the belt itself is the Lifecycle Rule.
Think of a delete marker as a curtain in front of the object: versioning keeps the object behind the curtain, and noncurrent-version expiration finally removes it.
Think of a prefix as a folder address and a tag as a label on the parcel — either can steer the rule.
edgeCases: Noncurrent version transitions/deletion only exist if versioning is enabled.
Incomplete multipart uploads consume storage until a rule expires them; clean them up explicitly.
Objects can be transitioned multiple times in sequence (Standard → Standard IA → Glacier Deep Archive) as in Scenario 2.
Lifecycle rules by tag require the tag to exist on the object to be matched.
An object can be both transitioned and expired by the same overall configuration when requirements differ per object set (source images vs thumbnails in Scenario 1).

whenToUse.situation: Objects are accessed rarely but must still be retrievable quickly.
Archive data that does not need fast access.
whenToUse.use: Transition to Glacier or Glacier Deep Archive.

whenToUse.situation: Log files older than 365 days are no longer needed.
whenToUse.use: Expiration action to delete access log files after 365 days.

whenToUse.situation: Versioned bucket accumulating old object versions.
Bucket has many abandoned multipart uploads.
whenToUse.use: Expiration action to delete incomplete multipart uploads.

whenToUse.situation: Only one application path's objects should be tiered.
Rules must follow objects across arbitrary key layouts, e.g. by department.
whenToUse.use: Rule scoped to a tag (Department: Finance).

whenToUse.situation: You don't know which objects are cold and want data-driven lifecycle design.
whenToUse.use: Start with S3 Storage Class Analysis, then build Lifecycle Rules from its report.

whenToUse.situation: Objects can be regenerated easily and are only needed 60 days.
whenToUse.use: Store in One-Zone IA and expire after 60 days.

patternsToRecognize.signal: "immediately retrievable for 60 days, then up to 6 hours"
patternsToRecognize.indicates: Standard (or Standard IA) for the immediate window, transition to Glacier afterwards.

patternsToRecognize.signal: "recover deleted objects immediately for 30 days, within 48 hours for up to 365 days"
patternsToRecognize.indicates: Versioning + noncurrent version transitions (Standard IA then Glacier Deep Archive).

patternsToRecognize.signal: "which service recommends when to transition objects"

patternsToRecognize.indicates: Expiration actions in a lifecycle rule.

examTraps.trap: S3 Analytics can be used for One-Zone IA and Glacier optimization.
examTraps.correction: Analysis recommendations cover only Standard and Standard IA; it does not work for One-Zone IA or Glacier.

examTraps.trap: Enabling versioning automatically deletes old versions.
examTraps.correction: Versioning retains versions; you must add noncurrent-version expiration/transition actions.

examTraps.trap: Lifecycle rules are a substitute for S3 Analytics.
examTraps.correction: They are complementary: Analytics informs the rules, the rules execute them.

examTraps.trap: Delete markers free the storage of overwritten objects.
examTraps.correction: Only expiring noncurrent versions removes the underlying versions.

examTraps.trap: Lifecycle rules cannot be targeted narrowly.
examTraps.correction: They can be filtered by prefix or by object tag.
It takes 24 to 48 hours to start seeing analysis, with daily report updates.

beyondSource: Current S3 lifecycle configurations often distinguish current-version and noncurrent-version actions explicitly (transition and expiration for each), which is consistent with the section's noncurrent-version scenarios.

Lifecycle rules support minimum object-age thresholds in whole days and are evaluated asynchronously, so transitions are not instantaneous at the exact day boundary; the exam generally tests the intended design rather than timing exactness.
